克羅姆管實際出現的音樂場合，可確認者為早期巴洛克時期的法國宮廷音樂。它的名稱常與: The musical settings in which the cromorne actually appears, as far as can be confirmed, are French court music of the early Baroque. Its name is often confused with another wooden wind reed instrument, the crumhorn; the crumhorn is a capped double-reed instrument, usually hooked in shape and narrow in range, found in the inventories of King Henry VIII and the Earl of Arundel, at Nonsuch House and in Sir William Leighton's verse, but rare among English town musicians and in French sources. So when listening for the cromorne, take early Baroque French court music as the context, and do not treat records of the crumhorn as records of the cromorne itself.

Its name is often confused with the crumhorn, a capped double-reed instrument that may be a different design and that 17th-century French theorists called the tournebout. The crumhorn is a capped double-reed instrument, usually J-shaped, with a range of about a ninth, extendable by keys or underblowing. 17th-century French theorists called it the tournebout, among them Mersenne (1636), Pierre Trichet (about 1640) and Diderot (1767). It seems little used in England and France: it appears in the inventory of Henry VIII and the Earl of Arundel at Nonsuch House and in Sir William Leighton's verse, yet not in the records of town musicians.
